courses.title: What is HTML?
courses.description:
> **Before this lesson,** you should be able to make a folder and a file in the terminal with `mkdir` and `touch`, and open a folder in VS Code with `code .` **HTML** is the language used to build every web page in the world. When you open any website, your browser is quietly reading HTML behind the scenes and turning it into the page you see. Do not worry about memorising anything today. We will build a real page together at the end of this lesson. ## HTML is made of tags An HTML page is built out of **tags**. A tag is a keyword wrapped in angle brackets, like this: `

`. Most tags come in a **pair** — an **opening** tag and a **closing** tag. The closing tag looks the same but has a slash `/` in front of the word: ```html

Hello world

``` Read that from left to right: *start a paragraph* (`

`), the text is *Hello world*, *end the paragraph* (`

`). The two tags wrap around the content like a box around it. Here `

` means **paragraph**. There are many other tags — `

` for a big heading, `` for a picture, and more. You will meet them one lesson at a time, so there is no rush. ## Tag, element, content — three words you will hear constantly People use these three words as if everyone already knows them, so here they are plainly: - A **tag** is one of the things in angle brackets: `

` is a tag, and so is `

`. - The **content** is what sits between them: *Hello world*. - An **element** is the whole thing together — opening tag, content, closing tag. ```html

Hello world

``` That whole line is **one element**. It is built from two **tags** with some **content** in between. So when a later lesson says *"give the element a class"* or *"select an element"*, it means the whole thing — not just the `

` part. Tag and element get used loosely in the wild, and now you know why. ## Some tags carry extra information Sometimes a tag needs to know more than just its text. That extra information goes **inside the opening tag** and is called an **attribute**. For example, a link needs to know *where* it should take you: ```html Click me ``` Here `` is a link, `href="https://example.com"` is the attribute that says where the link goes, and *Click me* is the text a person actually clicks. Do not worry about links yet — there is a whole lesson on them later. This is just to show you what an attribute looks like. ## Let us build your first page together This is a **practice page**, just for trying things out — it is not the assignment. Your assignments work differently: each one arrives as its own folder with `index.html`, `style.css` and `script.js` already made for you, and you open those and edit them. Here you are making a file from nothing, once, so you can see where a web page actually comes from. Follow along, step by step. ### Step 1 — Open the terminal in your course folder 1. Click the **yellow folder icon** on the bar at the bottom of your screen (**File Explorer**). 2. Click **Documents**, then double-click **`lacefi-academy`**. 3. **Right-click** on empty white space inside it → **Show more options** → **Open Git Bash here**. *(On a Mac: press **Command + Space**, type `Terminal`, press **Enter**, then type `cd ~/Documents/lacefi-academy` and press **Enter**.)* ### Step 2 — Make a practice folder and a file Type these three lines, pressing **Enter** after each: ```bash mkdir mypage cd mypage touch index.html ``` You just made a folder called `mypage` inside your course folder, stepped into it, and made an empty file called `index.html`. (`index.html` is a special name — it is the file a browser looks for first.) This `mypage` folder is yours to play in. Nothing here is graded, and you can delete it whenever you like. ### Step 3 — Open it in VS Code ```bash code . ``` VS Code opens. Down the left-hand side you will see your file. **Click once on `index.html`** to open it in the big area on the right. ### Step 4 — Type some HTML Type this into the file, then **save it: press Ctrl + S** *(Mac: Command + S)*. If the tab at the top of VS Code shows a white dot instead of an ✕, it is **not saved** — press Ctrl + S again. ```html

My first web page

Hi, I made this all by myself!

``` `

` is a big heading. `

` is a paragraph. That is a complete little page. ### Step 5 — See it in your browser 1. In VS Code, **right-click `index.html`** in the file list on the left. 2. Click **Reveal in File Explorer** *(Mac: **Reveal in Finder**)*. 3. **Double-click `index.html`**. It opens in your web browser, and you see your heading and your paragraph on the screen. **This is the loop you will repeat for the rest of the course:** change the file in VS Code → press **Ctrl + S** to save → click back to the browser → press **Ctrl + R** to reload → look at what changed. Try it now: change the words in your `

`, save, reload, and watch the page follow you. **You just built a web page.** Everything from here is simply learning more tags to put inside it. Do the small task below to practise, then move on to the next lesson. ## Recap — the short version - Most tags come in a pair, and the closing one carries a slash: `

` opens it, `

` closes it. A forgotten slash is the most common first mistake. - A **tag** is the part in angle brackets, the **content** is what sits between the tags, and the **element** is all of it together. - An **attribute** goes inside the opening tag and gives it extra information, like `href="https://example.com"` on a link. - `index.html` is a special file name — it is the one a browser looks for first. - The loop never changes: edit the file, **Ctrl + S** to save, click back to the browser, **Ctrl + R** to reload.

` heading and a `

` paragraph, and save with **Ctrl + S**

Push your work, then submit with a tag

courses.title: The shape of every page
courses.description:
> **Before this lesson,** you should be able to write a heading and a paragraph in an `index.html` file and open that file in your browser Every real web page starts from the same little skeleton. Copy it, then fill in the middle. Here it is: ```html My Page

Hello

``` What each part means, in plain words: - `` — tells the browser *this is a modern web page*. Always the first line. - `` — wraps the whole page. `lang="en"` just says the page is in English. - `` — information **about** the page that visitors do not see: the character set, screen settings, and the `` (the name shown on the browser tab). - `<body>` — everything people actually **see**: your headings, text, images, and so on. From now on, put your work inside the `<body>`. ## Where you will see this happen Most of this skeleton is invisible on the page, so it can look as though nothing happened. The `<title>` is the part you can actually check. 1. Save the file with **Ctrl + S** *(Mac: **Command + S**)*. 2. **Right-click `index.html`** in VS Code's file list → **Reveal in File Explorer** *(Mac: **Reveal in Finder**)*. 3. **Double-click** `index.html` to open it in your browser. 4. Look at the **tab** at the very top of the browser window, not at the page. The words you put inside `<title>` are printed there. The `<body>` is the only part that shows on the page itself. Change the `<title>`, press **Ctrl + S**, click back to the browser and press **Ctrl + R** — the tab name follows you. ## Recap — the short version - `<!doctype html>` is always the very first line, with nothing above it. - Everything a visitor sees goes inside `<body>`. The `<head>` holds information **about** the page, so nothing you put there appears on the page. - The `<title>` shows on the browser **tab**, not on the page. - The skeleton nests: `<html>` wraps `<head>` and `<body>`, and each of them needs its closing tag.

Change the `<title>` to your own page name
Put an `<h1>` heading inside the `<body>`, save with **Ctrl + S**, and open the file in your browser
Push your work, then submit with a tag

courses.description:
> **Before this lesson,** you should be able to write the ``, `` and `` skeleton of a page Most of a web page is text. Two tags do the heavy lifting: headings and paragraphs. **Real example:** open any news story on `https://www.bbc.com/news`. Notice the big **headline** at the top, the smaller **section titles**, and the **paragraphs** of the story. That is exactly what you are about to build. ## Headings Headings are titles. There are six sizes, from `

` (biggest) down to `

` (smallest). Use **one** `

` for the main title of the page, then `

` for the sections beneath it, like the chapters of a book: ```html

My Cooking Blog

Breakfast

Dinner

``` Do not pick a heading just because of its size — pick it for its **meaning** (main title, then section, then sub-section). This is how screen readers and Google understand your page. ## Paragraphs A paragraph is a block of normal text, wrapped in `

`: ```html

This is my first paragraph.

And this is a second one.

``` ## Making words stand out - `` marks text as **important** (browsers show it bold). - `` adds **emphasis** (browsers show it in italics). ```html

This is really important and a little exciting.

``` **Try it:** on your page, add an `

` with your name, an `

` called *About me*, and a paragraph under it. Make one word ``. ## Recap — the short version - Use one `

` for the page, then `

` for its sections. Pick a heading for its meaning, not because you like its size. - There are six heading levels, `

` down to `

`, and `

` is the biggest. - `` marks text as important and shows bold; `` adds emphasis and shows italic. Both need a closing tag. - Every paragraph needs its own `

` element. Pressing Enter twice in the file does not make a new paragraph.

courses.title: Links
courses.description: > **Before this lesson,** you should be able to write headings and paragraphs, and mark a word as important with `` Links are what turn a pile of separate pages into a **web**. Every time you click a word and jump somewhere new, that is a link doing its job. **Real example:** open Wikipedia at `https://en.wikipedia.org` and click any blue word inside an article. Every single one is a link. That is the whole idea of the web in one page — go try it. ## Making a link You make a link with the `` tag (the *a* stands for *anchor*) and its `href` attribute — the address it points to: ```html Go to Wikipedia ``` The words between the tags (*Go to Wikipedia*) are what a person clicks. The `href` is where they land. ## Three links you will use all the time - **To another website** — use the full address: ```html Google ``` - **To another page in your own project** — just the file name: ```html About me ``` - **To open in a new tab** — add `target="_blank"`: ```html Open Google in a new tab ``` **Try it:** add a link to your favourite website on your page, save, and click it in your browser. Then make a second link that opens in a new tab. ## Recap — the short version - The address goes in the `href` attribute inside the opening tag. The words people click go between `` and ``. - A link to another website needs the full address including `https://`. Leave it off and the browser hunts for a file in your own folder instead. - A link to one of your own pages needs only the file name, like `about.html`. - `target="_blank"` makes the link open in a new tab.

Add a second link with `target="_blank"` so it opens in a new tab

Push your work, then submit with a tag

courses.title: Images
courses.description: > **Before this lesson,** you should be able to add a link with `` and point its `href` at a web address A page of only text is dull. Images bring it to life. **Real example:** open Unsplash at `https://unsplash.com` — it is a giant wall of photos, and every one is an HTML image. You can even grab a free photo there to use on your own page later. ## Adding an image Use the `` tag. It is a lonely tag — no closing partner needed: ```html ``` Two attributes matter: - `src` — the **source**: where the picture is. This can be a file on your computer (`cat.jpg`) or a full web address (`https://.../cat.jpg`). - `alt` — the **alternative text**: a short description of the picture in words. It is read aloud to people who cannot see the image, and it shows if the picture fails to load. **Always** write a clear, honest alt. Good alt: `alt="A red bicycle leaning on a brick wall"`. Lazy alt: `alt="image"` (do not do this). ## Adding a caption Wrap the image and a caption together: ```html ``` **Try it:** download a photo from `https://unsplash.com`, save it next to your `index.html`, and show it on your page with a clear `alt`. ## Recap — the short version - `` has no closing tag. It is written on its own: ``. - `src` is where the picture is. A plain file name means *next to my `index.html`*, so the photo has to sit in the same folder. - `alt` is a short honest description. It is read aloud to people who cannot see the picture, and it shows if the picture fails to load. - `

The **ingredients** are a bullet list (order does not matter). The **method** is a numbered list (order absolutely matters — you cannot bake before you mix). Same idea you are about to use. ## Unordered list (bullets) Use `
    ` when the order does not matter: ```html
    • Bread
    • Milk

courses.title: Welcome to LaceFi Academy
courses.description:
> **Before this lesson,** you should be able to switch on your computer and open a web browser

This is where you learn by **doing**. Here is how it all works.

**Courses and modules.** The **Courses** tab on the left is your curriculum, grouped into modules. Modules unlock in order — finish one to open the next. Open any course to see a short explanation, sometimes a video, and a checklist of steps.

**Watch, then build.** Read the lesson, watch the video if there is one, and work through the steps on your own computer.

**Two simple actions: push and submit.** Each course ends with an assignment. When you accept it you get your OWN private GitHub repository. As you work, **push** often to save your progress online:

```bash
git add .
git commit -m "My work"
git push
```

Pushing is free and does not grade you. When you are ready for the robot to check your work, **submit** it with a tag:

```bash
git tag submit/1
git push origin submit/1
```

The robot (GitHub Actions) then checks each requirement and marks it with a check or a cross. Fix and submit again (`submit/2`, `submit/3`, …) until everything passes.

**Your progress.** A course shows a green check once you pass its assignment, and it all rolls up on your progress.

Take the quick quiz below to make sure it clicked, then start **Getting Started**.

## Recap — the short version

- Pushing and submitting are not the same thing: `git push` saves your work online and grades nothing, while a `submit/1` tag is what asks the robot to check it.
- Every assignment gives you your own private GitHub repository, which you clone onto your computer before you start work.
- If a requirement comes back with a cross, fix your code and submit again with the next number — `submit/2`, then `submit/3`.
- Modules unlock in order, so a course opens only once you have passed the one before it.

courses.title: Set up your computer
courses.description:
> **Before this lesson,** you should be able to find your way around a web browser and type a website address

Before you can build a website, you need a few free tools on your computer. This lesson helps you install each one. Do not rush — install one, check it worked, then move to the next. Doing this carefully now saves you trouble later.

## Tool 1 — VS Code (where you write your code)

VS Code is a free app for writing code. It is a bit like a word processor, but built for code instead of essays.

1. Open your web browser and go to `https://code.visualstudio.com`.
2. Click the big blue **Download** button. The website knows whether you are on Windows or Mac and gives you the right file.
3. Open the file you just downloaded and install it — click **Next** or **Install** and accept the normal choices.
4. When it finishes, open VS Code once to make sure it works. You can close it again after.

## Tool 2 — A terminal and Git

The **terminal** is a window where you type commands (you will meet it properly in the very next lesson). You also need **Git**, a small tool that saves your code and sends it online.

**On Windows**, one single download gives you both the terminal and Git. It is called **Git Bash**.

1. Go to `https://git-scm.com/download/win`.
2. The download starts by itself after a moment. Open the file when it is done.
3. An installer opens with many screens. Just keep clicking **Next** and accept every default choice — you do not need to change anything.
4. When it finishes, you will have an app called **Git Bash** in your Start menu. That is your terminal.

**On Mac**, you already have a terminal (an app called **Terminal**), and Git usually comes with it. You do not need to install anything in this step.

## Tool 3 — A GitHub account (where your code lives online)

GitHub is a website that stores your code online and, on this platform, checks your work for you.

1. Go to `https://github.com`.
2. Click **Sign up** and follow the steps — you choose a username, enter an email, and pick a password.
3. It is completely free. **Write your username down** somewhere safe, because you will need it soon.

## Tool 4 — The GitHub CLI (so your computer can talk to GitHub)

The **GitHub CLI** is a small tool called `gh`. It connects the Git on your computer to your GitHub account, so that when you send your work online you are not asked for a password every time. Setting it up once now makes everything later much smoother.

**Install it:**

1. Go to `https://cli.github.com`.
2. Click **Download for Windows** (or Mac). Open the file and install it, accepting the defaults.
3. Close and re-open your terminal (Git Bash on Windows, Terminal on Mac) so it notices the new tool.

**Log in — this connects `gh` to your account:**

1. In your terminal, type this and press Enter:

   ```bash
   gh auth login
   ```

2. It asks a few questions. Answer with the arrow keys and Enter:
   - *Where do you use GitHub?* → **GitHub.com**
   - *Preferred protocol?* → **HTTPS**
   - *Authenticate Git with your GitHub credentials?* → **Yes**
   - *How would you like to authenticate?* → **Login with a web browser**
3. It shows a short **one-time code** (like `A1B2-C3D4`). Copy it, press Enter, and your browser opens. Paste the code and click **Authorize**.
4. Back in the terminal you will see **✓ Logged in**. That is it — you only ever do this once.

You can check it worked any time by typing `gh auth status`.

## Your checklist

- VS Code installed and opened once.
- Windows: Git Bash installed. Mac: you found the Terminal app.
- GitHub account created, username written down.
- GitHub CLI (`gh`) installed and logged in (`gh auth status` shows a ✓).

When all of these are done, open the next lesson: **Meet the terminal**.

## Recap — the short version

- You run `gh auth login` once, and once only. Check it any time afterwards with `gh auth status`, which answers with a ✓.
- On Windows, **Git Bash** is one download that gives you both a terminal and Git. On a Mac, **Terminal** is already installed and Git usually comes with it.

courses.title: Meet the terminal
courses.description:
> **Before this lesson,** you should be able to install VS Code and open Git Bash on Windows, or Terminal on a Mac

The **terminal** is simply a window where you talk to your computer by **typing** instead of clicking. That is all it is. You type one short instruction, press **Enter**, and the computer does it.

It looks plain and a little scary the first time. That is completely normal. You will only ever need about five commands, and you **cannot break your computer** by trying them here. Let us go slowly, one step at a time.

## Step 1 — Make one folder for the whole course

Everything you build in this course will live in **one folder** on your computer, so your work stays tidy and easy to find. Let us make it now.

1. Open **File Explorer** (the yellow folder icon on your taskbar).
2. On the left, click **Documents**.
3. Right-click on an empty white space → **New** → **Folder**.
4. Name the new folder **`lacefi-academy`** and press **Enter**.

That is it. From now on, **every assignment you clone goes inside `Documents\lacefi-academy`**. (On a Mac it is the same: make a `lacefi-academy` folder inside your Documents.)

## Step 2 — Open the terminal *inside* that folder

Here is the easiest way to open the terminal already pointing at your folder — do it this way and you will avoid a lot of confusion.

**On Windows:**

1. Open your **`Documents\lacefi-academy`** folder in File Explorer.
2. **Right-click** on an empty white space inside the folder.
3. Click **Show more options** (on Windows 11), then click **Open Git Bash here**.

A window opens with some text and a **blinking cursor** — and it is already inside your `lacefi-academy` folder. (That blinking cursor is the computer waiting for you to type.)

*(If you don't see "Open Git Bash here", you may not have installed Git Bash yet — go back to the "Set up your computer" lesson.)*

**On Mac:** open the **Terminal** app (press **Command + Space**, type *Terminal*, press Enter), then type `cd ~/Documents/lacefi-academy` and press Enter to move into your folder.

## Step 3 — What you are looking at

The line with the blinking cursor is called the **prompt** — the computer quietly saying *I am ready, tell me what to do.* You type a command there, press **Enter**, and it runs. You barely touch the mouse in here — just type, then Enter.

## Step 4 — Where am I? (`pwd`)

Type this exactly, then press **Enter**:

```bash
pwd
```

`pwd` means *print working directory*. It shows the folder you are in right now — you should see it ends with `lacefi-academy`. That is *where am I?* answered.

## Step 5 — What is here? (`ls`)

```bash
ls
```

`ls` means *list*. It shows the files and folders where you are — like opening a drawer to see what is inside. (Your folder is empty for now, so you may see nothing. That is fine.)

## Step 6 — Move around (`cd`)

`cd` means *change directory* (directory is just another word for folder). To go **into** a folder, type `cd` then its name:

```bash
cd practice
```

To go **back out** one step:

```bash
cd ..
```

The two dots mean *the folder just above this one*.

## Step 7 — Make a folder (`mkdir`)

```bash
mkdir practice
```

`mkdir` means *make directory*. Type `ls` again and your new `practice` folder appears.

## Step 8 — Make a file (`touch`)

```bash
touch notes.txt
```

`touch` makes a new empty file. You now know how to make folders and files from the keyboard.

## Step 9 — Open the folder in VS Code (`code .`)

When you want to write code in the folder you are in, type:

```bash
code .
```

The dot means *this folder, the one I am in now*. VS Code opens, ready to edit.

## That is it — your whole toolkit

- `pwd` — where am I?
- `ls` — what is here?
- `cd name` — go into a folder. `cd ..` — go back out.
- `mkdir name` — make a folder.
- `touch name` — make a file.
- `code .` — open this folder in VS Code.

**Remember the big habit:** open your `lacefi-academy` folder, right-click, **Open Git Bash here** — and you're ready to work. You'll do this at the start of every assignment.

**Try it:** open Git Bash inside your `lacefi-academy` folder, run `pwd`, then `mkdir practice`, then `cd practice`, then `ls`. Go slowly — you cannot break anything.

## Recap — the short version

- `cd ..` — two dots — takes you back **out** one folder. `cd name` takes you **into** one.
- The dot in `code .` means *this folder, the one I am in right now*.
- `pwd` says where you are, `ls` says what is here, `mkdir` makes a folder and `touch` makes a file.
- Opening the terminal by right-clicking inside a folder means it already points at that folder, which avoids most early confusion.
- A command only runs when you press **Enter**, and nothing you type in here can break your computer.

Run `pwd`, then `mkdir practice`, then `cd practice`, then `ls`, pressing **Enter** after each

courses.title: What is CSS?
courses.description:
> **Before this lesson,** you should be able to write an HTML page and add tags inside its `<head>`

HTML builds the **structure** of a page. **CSS** makes it **beautiful** — colours, fonts, spacing, layout. If HTML is the skeleton, CSS is the skin, hair, and clothes.

**Real example:** open `https://www.csszengarden.com`. Every design on that page uses the *exact same HTML* — only the CSS changes. That is the power of CSS: same bones, endless looks.

## How to add CSS

The tidy way is a separate file. Make a file called `style.css` next to your `index.html`, then link it inside the `<head>` of your HTML:

```html
<head>
  <link rel="stylesheet" href="style.css">
</head>
```

Now anything you write in `style.css` styles your page.

## A CSS rule

CSS is made of **rules**. Each rule picks something and gives it a look:

```css
h1 {
  color: blue;
  font-size: 40px;
}
```

Read it as: *find every `<h1>`, and make its text blue and 40 pixels big.*

- `h1` is the **selector** — what to style.
- `color` and `font-size` are **properties** — what to change.
- `blue` and `40px` are the **values**.
- The curly braces `{ }` hold the rules, and every line ends with a semicolon `;`.

**Try it:** make a `style.css`, link it from your HTML, and turn your `<h1>` a colour you like.

## Where you will see this happen

1. Save both files with **Ctrl + S**.
2. **Right-click `index.html`** in VS Code → **Reveal in File Explorer** *(Mac: **Reveal in Finder**)* → **double-click** it.
3. Your `<h1>` should now be the colour you chose. Nothing else on the page changes, so this one heading is the whole proof.
4. If the heading is still plain black, the stylesheet is not linked. Open `index.html` and check that `<link rel="stylesheet" href="style.css">` sits inside `<head>`, spelled exactly, and that your file really is called `style.css`.
5. After every edit: save with **Ctrl + S**, click back to the browser, press **Ctrl + R**.

## Recap — the short version

- CSS in `style.css` does nothing at all until `<link rel="stylesheet" href="style.css">` sits inside the `<head>` of your HTML — a typo in that file name leaves the page completely unstyled.
- A rule has the shape `selector { property: value; }`: the selector picks what to style, and everything you want to change goes inside the curly braces `{ }`.
- A colon `:` sits between the property and the value, and a semicolon `;` ends every declaration.
- CSS uses American spelling: the property is `color`, never `colour`, and the browser quietly ignores a property name it does not recognise.
- Same HTML with different CSS gives a completely different-looking page — that is what `csszengarden.com` demonstrates.

Colour is the fastest way to make a page feel alive.

**Real example:** open `https://coolors.co` and press the spacebar to generate a colour palette. Those are exactly the kinds of colours you can drop into CSS.

## Two colour properties

- `color` — the colour of **text**.
- `background-color` — the colour **behind** an element.

```css
body {
  background-color: #f5f5f5;
}
h1 {
  color: crimson;
}
```

## Ways to write a colour

- **Names:** `red`, `blue`, `crimson`, `teal` (about 140 names exist).
- **Hex codes:** `#ff0000` is red, `#00b894` is green. They start with `#` and let you pick *any* colour. You copy these straight from a site like Coolors.

**Try it:** give your whole page a soft `background-color` on the `body`, and make your `<h1>` a bold `color`.

## Recap — the short version

- `color` sets the colour of the text, and `background-color` sets the colour behind the element — swapping the two is the usual reason a box comes out the wrong colour.
- Both are spelled the American way. `colour` is not a CSS property, and a misspelt property is ignored without any warning.
- A hex code starts with a hash, like `#00b894`; a colour name like `crimson` takes no hash.
- Set the page background on `body` so it covers the whole page rather than one box.
- A palette site such as `coolors.co` gives you hex codes you can paste straight into your CSS.

Good-looking text makes a page easy and pleasant to read.

**Real example:** notice how articles on `https://medium.com` use a clean, large, well-spaced font with lots of breathing room. That is all CSS.

## The main text properties

```css
p {
  font-family: Arial, sans-serif;
  font-size: 18px;
  font-weight: bold;
  text-align: center;
  color: #333;
}
```

- `font-family` — which font to use. List a backup, ending in `sans-serif` (plain) or `serif` (with little feet).
- `font-size` — how big, e.g. `18px`.
- `font-weight` — `normal` or `bold`.
- `text-align` — `left`, `center`, or `right`.
- `color` — the text colour.

A comfy trick for readable body text: `font-size: 18px` and a dark grey like `#333` instead of pure black.

**Try it:** set a nice `font-family` on your `body`, make paragraphs `18px`, and centre your `<h1>` with `text-align`.

## Recap — the short version

- `text-align: center` is spelled the American way — `centre` does nothing at all, and the browser gives you no warning.
- `color` sets the colour of the text, and it is the American spelling here too.
- `font-family` takes a list, and the browser uses the first font it actually has, so end the list with `sans-serif` or `serif`.
- `text-align` moves text inside its own box, so the box has to be wider than the text for the change to show.
- Body text at `18px` in a dark grey such as `#333` is more comfortable to read than small pure-black text.

Here is the secret to spacing and layout: **every element on a page is a box.** Once you see the box, you can control the space everywhere.

**Real example:** on any website, right-click something and choose **Inspect**, then hover over the element. You will see a coloured diagram — blue content, green padding, orange margin. That is the box model.

## The four parts, from inside out

- **content** — the text or image itself.
- **padding** — space *inside* the box, between the content and the border.
- **border** — a line drawn around the box.
- **margin** — space *outside* the box, pushing other things away.

```css
.card {
  width: 300px;
  padding: 20px;
  border: 2px solid gray;
  margin: 16px;
}
```

Think of a framed photo on a wall: the photo is the **content**, the white mount around it is the **padding**, the wooden frame is the **border**, and the gap to the next frame is the **margin**.

**Try it:** put a `border`, some `padding`, and a `margin` on a `<div>` in your page and watch the space appear around it.

## Recap — the short version

- Padding is the space **inside** the border and margin is the space **outside** it — that one distinction explains most spacing problems you will hit.
- Every element on a page is a box with four parts, from the inside out: content, padding, border, margin.
- Right-click an element and choose **Inspect** to see the box drawn in colour: blue content, green padding, orange margin.
- `border: 2px solid gray;` gives the width, the style and the colour in one go, in that order.
- Picture a framed photo: the photo is the content, the mount is the padding, the frame is the border, and the gap to the next frame is the margin.

courses.title: Introduction to JavaScript
courses.description:
> **Before this lesson,** you should be able to style a whole page with CSS rules you wrote yourself

**JavaScript** is the language that makes web pages *do things*. If HTML is the structure of a page and CSS is how it looks, then JavaScript is the **behaviour** — the part that reacts, changes, and responds to the person using it.

## What can JavaScript do?

Almost everything interactive you have ever seen on a website:

- Show or hide things when you click a button.
- Check a form before it is sent ("your password is too short").
- Update part of a page without reloading it (like a live search).
- Build whole apps — chat, maps, games, spreadsheets.

The same language also runs outside the browser (on servers, phones, even robots), so learning it opens a lot of doors. But we start where it began: in the web page.

## Three languages, one team

Think of a button on a website:

- **HTML** creates the button — `<button>Buy now</button>`.
- **CSS** makes it look good — round corners, a nice colour.
- **JavaScript** makes it work — when you click, something happens.

You already know the first two. JavaScript is the third and final piece.

## Your very first line

The simplest thing JavaScript can do is print a message to the **console** — a hidden panel in the browser built for developers. Here is a complete example:

```javascript
console.log("Hello from JavaScript!");
```

`console.log(...)` means *print whatever is in the brackets to the console*. It is the tool you will use most while learning, because it lets you peek at what your code is doing.

## See it yourself

1. Open any web page in your browser.
2. Press **F12** (or right-click → **Inspect**) to open the developer tools.
3. Click the **Console** tab.
4. Type `console.log("Hi!")` and press Enter.

You just ran JavaScript. In the next lessons you will learn where to put your code, and how to make it do more than say hello.

**Try it:** open the console on any page and `console.log` your own name.

## Where you will see this happen

JavaScript does not print onto the page. It prints into the **Console** — a panel that stays hidden until you ask for it.

1. Open any web page in your browser.
2. Press **F12** *(Mac: **Command + Option + J**)*. A panel opens at the side or the bottom of the window.
3. Click the **Console** tab along the top of that panel.
4. Click in the empty space next to the `>` sign, type `console.log("Hi!")` and press **Enter**.

`Hi!` appears on the next line. That is JavaScript running.

The Console stays open while you work. When you are running your own file, the habit is always the same: save with **Ctrl + S**, click back to the browser, press **Ctrl + R** to reload.

## Recap — the short version

- The Console is hidden until you press **F12** and click the **Console** tab. Nothing on the page itself changes when you `console.log`, so a blank-looking page does not mean your code failed.
- `console.log(...)` prints whatever is inside the brackets to the Console. It is the tool you will use most while learning, because it lets you see what your code is doing.
- HTML is the structure, CSS is the look, JavaScript is the behaviour — the part that reacts when someone clicks, types or scrolls.
- Text you print sits inside quotes and the statement ends with a semicolon: `console.log("Hello");`.

courses.title: Variables: let and const
courses.description:
> **Before this lesson,** you should be able to write JavaScript statements ending in semicolons and add `//` comments

A **variable** is a named box that holds a value. You put something in the box, give the box a name, and use that name later. Variables are how programs remember things.

## Making a variable

Use the word `let`, a name, an `=`, and a value:

```javascript
let age = 12;
let name = "Ada";
```

Read `=` as *"gets"*, not *"equals"*: `age` **gets** the value 12. Now anywhere you write `age`, JavaScript sees 12:

```javascript
console.log(age);        // 12
console.log(name);       // Ada
```

## Changing a variable

With `let`, you can change the value later — just use the name again, no second `let`:

```javascript
let score = 0;
score = 10;
score = score + 5;
console.log(score);      // 15
```

That last line looks strange but is very common: it means *take the current score, add 5, and put the result back in score.*

## `const` — a box you won't change

If a value should **never change**, use `const` instead of `let`:

```javascript
const pi = 3.14159;
const birthYear = 2010;
```

Try to change a `const` and JavaScript stops you with an error. This is a good thing — it protects values that are meant to stay fixed. A simple rule: **use `const` by default, and `let` only when you know the value will change.**

## `var` — the old way

You may see `var` in older code. It works but has confusing quirks. In modern JavaScript we use `let` and `const`. Just recognise `var` when you see it.

## Naming your boxes

- Start with a letter. Use camelCase: `firstName`, `totalPrice`.
- Make names describe the value: `age` is better than `a`.
- Remember capitals matter: `age` and `Age` are different boxes.

**Try it:** make a `const` for your name and a `let` for your age, `console.log` both, then change the age and log it again.

## Where you will see this happen

Save with **Ctrl + S**, click back to the browser, press **Ctrl + R**. *(Console closed? Press **F12**, then the **Console** tab — Mac: **Command + Option + J**.)*

The Console shows one line for each `console.log`, in the order they ran. That is why logging the same variable twice is worth doing: the first line shows the old value, the second shows the new one after you changed it. One name, two values, a moment apart.

## Recap — the short version

- Read `=` as *gets*, not *equals*: `let age = 12` puts 12 into the box called `age`.
- Use `const` by default and `let` only when you know the value will change. Trying to change a `const` stops the program with an error.
- To change a `let`, use the name on its own — `score = 10`, with no second `let`.
- `score = score + 5` means take the current score, add 5, and put the result back in `score`.
- `var` is the old way of making a variable. Recognise it in older code, but write `let` and `const`.

courses.title: Functions
courses.description:
> **Before this lesson,** you should be able to write a `for ... of` loop over an array and `console.log` each item

A **function** is a reusable block of code — a little machine you build once and run whenever you like. Functions are how you avoid repeating yourself and how you organise a program into named steps.

## Defining a function

Use the word `function`, a name, brackets, and a block:

```javascript
function sayHello() {
  console.log("Hello!");
}
```

Writing this does **not** run it — it just defines the machine. To run it, **call** it by name with brackets:

```javascript
sayHello();     // Hello!
sayHello();     // Hello!  — run it as often as you like
```

## Inputs: parameters

Most functions take **inputs** so they can do different things each time. Inputs go in the brackets and are called *parameters*:

```javascript
function greet(name) {
  console.log("Hello, " + name + "!");
}

greet("Ada");     // Hello, Ada!
greet("Grace");   // Hello, Grace!
```

`name` is a placeholder; the real value you pass in ("Ada") is the *argument*. You can have several:

```javascript
function add(a, b) {
  console.log(a + b);
}
add(3, 4);   // 7
```

## Output: return

`console.log` *shows* a value; **`return`** *hands a value back* so the rest of your program can use it:

```javascript
function add(a, b) {
  return a + b;
}

let total = add(3, 4);
console.log(total);        // 7
console.log(add(10, 5));   // 15
```

The difference matters: a function that `return`s a total can feed that total into more maths. A function that only `console.log`s it can't. As a rule, **calculate with `return`, and `console.log` only to peek.**

Once a function hits `return`, it stops — nothing after it runs.

## Why functions are everywhere

Every button click, every calculation, every step of a big app is a function. Name them well (`calculateTotal`, `showError`) and your code reads like a set of instructions.

**Try it:** write a function `double(n)` that **returns** `n * 2`, then `console.log(double(8))`.

## Recap — the short version

- Writing a function does not run it. It runs only when you call it by name with brackets after it: `sayHello();`
- `return` hands a value back so the rest of your program can use it. `console.log` only shows it on the screen.
- Once a function reaches `return` it stops — nothing written after that line runs.
- The names in the brackets of the definition are parameters (placeholders). The real values you pass in when you call it are arguments.
- Name functions after what they do — `calculateTotal`, `showError` — and your code reads like a set of instructions.

courses.title: Events: reacting to clicks
courses.description:
> **Before this lesson,** you should be able to change an element's text, style or classes from `script.js`

An **event** is something that happens on the page — a click, a key press, a mouse hover, a form submit. JavaScript can **listen** for an event and run code when it happens. This is what makes a page truly interactive: it *reacts* to the person using it.

## Listen for a click

Start with a button:

```html
<button id="myButton">Click me</button>
```

Then in `script.js`, select it and attach a listener:

```javascript
const button = document.querySelector("#myButton");

button.addEventListener("click", function () {
  console.log("You clicked me!");
});
```

Read it as: *"On the button, listen for a **click**; when it happens, run this function."* Click the button and watch the console.

The function you pass in only runs **later**, each time the event fires. This is a big shift from top-to-bottom code: you're setting up a *reaction* and waiting.

## Make the click change the page

Combine events with the DOM changes you just learned:

```javascript
const button = document.querySelector("#myButton");
const title  = document.querySelector("#title");

button.addEventListener("click", function () {
  title.textContent = "You clicked!";
  title.style.color = "green";
});
```

Now clicking the button rewrites and recolours the heading. That's a real, interactive web page — built from pieces you already know.

## Other common events

The pattern is always `element.addEventListener("eventName", function)`. Swap the name:

- `"click"` — a click
- `"mouseover"` / `"mouseout"` — pointer enters / leaves
- `"keydown"` — a key is pressed
- `"input"` — the value of a text box changes
- `"submit"` — a form is submitted (next lesson)

## The everyday pattern

1. **Select** the element.
2. **`addEventListener`** with an event name.
3. In the function, **do something** (change the DOM, run a calculation…).

Master this and you can build almost any interaction.

**Try it:** add a button and, when it's clicked, change your heading's text (or colour).

## Recap — the short version

- Hand the function to `addEventListener` **without brackets after it**. Brackets would run it immediately instead of saving it for later.
- The event name is a string in quotes and all lower case: `"click"`, not `"Click"`.
- The code inside the listener runs each time the event happens, which may be long after the rest of your script has finished.
- The pattern never changes: select the element, `addEventListener` with an event name, then change something inside the function.
- Swap the name for a different reaction: `"mouseover"`, `"keydown"`, `"input"`, `"submit"`.

courses.title: Loops: for and while
courses.description:
> **Before this lesson,** you should be able to match one value against several options with `switch`, `case` and `default`

Sometimes you want to do the same thing many times without writing it out over and over. That is what a **loop** is for. Loops are one of the biggest reasons computers are useful — they never get bored.

## The `for` loop

The most common loop. It repeats a block a set number of times:

```javascript
for (let i = 1; i <= 5; i = i + 1) {
  console.log(i);
}
```

This prints 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. The three parts inside the brackets control it:

- `let i = 1` — **start**: begin counting at 1.
- `i <= 5` — **keep-going test**: repeat while this is true.
- `i = i + 1` — **step**: what happens after each round (here, add 1).

`i` is just a variable (short for *index*). Change the numbers and it counts differently. You'll often see the shorter `i++`, which means exactly the same as `i = i + 1`.

## The `while` loop

A `while` loop repeats *as long as* something is true. Use it when you don't know the exact count in advance:

```javascript
let count = 3;
while (count > 0) {
  console.log(count);
  count = count - 1;
}
console.log("Lift off!");
```

**Careful:** something inside the loop must eventually make the test false (here, `count` shrinks). If it never does, the loop runs forever — an "infinite loop."

## Stopping and skipping

- `break` — jump out of the loop completely.
- `continue` — skip the rest of this round and go to the next.

```javascript
for (let i = 1; i <= 10; i++) {
  if (i === 5) break;      // stop entirely at 5
  console.log(i);          // prints 1 2 3 4
}
```

## Why loops matter

A loop like this is how a web page shows a list of 100 products without you typing 100 lines — it just repeats the same step for each item. In the next lesson you'll loop straight over lists of things.

**Try it:** write a `for` loop that `console.log`s the numbers 1 to 10, then a `while` loop that counts down from 5 to 1.

## Recap — the short version

- An infinite loop happens when the test never becomes false. The tab freezes: nothing prints, clicks do nothing, and the page stops responding. Close that browser tab, fix the line that should change the counter, then open the page again.
- A `for` loop's brackets hold three parts separated by semicolons — where to start, how long to keep going, and what to change each round: `for (let i = 1; i <= 5; i++)`.
- `i++` means exactly the same as `i = i + 1`.
- Use `for` when you know how many rounds you need, and `while` when you only know the condition to stop on.
- `break` leaves the loop completely; `continue` skips the rest of this round and starts the next.

courses.title: JavaScript syntax
courses.description:
> **Before this lesson,** you should be able to link a `script.js` file to a page and print a message to the Console

Every language has rules for how you write it — its **syntax**. JavaScript's rules are simple, and knowing them now saves you from confusing errors later.

## Statements

A **statement** is one instruction. JavaScript runs your statements one at a time, top to bottom. Each usually sits on its own line and ends with a semicolon `;`:

```javascript
let name = "Ada";
console.log(name);
```

The semicolon is like a full stop at the end of a sentence. JavaScript can often guess where a statement ends without it, but adding it is a good, clear habit.

## JavaScript is case-sensitive

Capital letters matter. `myName`, `myname`, and `MyName` are **three different things**:

```javascript
let color = "red";
console.log(Color);   // Error! There is no "Color" (capital C)
```

Most JavaScript names use **camelCase**: start lowercase, then capitalise each new word — `firstName`, `totalPrice`, `isLoggedIn`.

## Spaces and lines

Extra spaces and blank lines are ignored, so you can lay code out to be readable:

```javascript
let price = 10;
let quantity = 3;
let total = price * quantity;
```

## Comments — notes that don't run

A **comment** is a note for humans; JavaScript skips it. Use them to explain *why* something is there.

```javascript
// This is a single-line comment

let taxRate = 0.16;   // 16% tax

/* This is a
   multi-line comment */
```

Anything after `//` on a line is ignored. Anything between `/*` and `*/` is ignored, even across many lines.

## Keywords

Some words are reserved for JavaScript itself — like `let`, `const`, `if`, `function`, `return`. You will learn each as you go; just know you can't use them as your own names.

**Try it:** in a `script.js`, write two statements that each `console.log` something, add a `// comment` above them explaining what they do, and run it.

## Where you will see this happen

Save `script.js` with **Ctrl + S**, click back to the browser and press **Ctrl + R** to reload. *(Console closed? Press **F12**, then the **Console** tab — Mac: **Command + Option + J**.)*

Both messages appear in the Console, one under the other, in the order you wrote them. Your `// comment` does not appear anywhere — that is correct. Comments are for people, and JavaScript skips them.

## Recap — the short version

- Capitals matter. `color`, `Color` and `COLOR` are three different names, and reaching for one that does not exist gives an error.
- One instruction is one statement, and each ends with a semicolon `;` — the full stop of code.
- Anything after `//` on a line is ignored, and anything between `/*` and `*/` is ignored even across many lines.
- Names are written in camelCase: start lower case, then capitalise each new word — `firstName`, `totalPrice`, `isLoggedIn`.
- Words such as `let`, `const`, `if`, `function` and `return` are reserved for JavaScript, so you cannot use them as your own names.

courses.title: Data types
courses.description:
> **Before this lesson,** you should be able to store values in variables with `let` and `const`

Variables can hold different *kinds* of values. These kinds are called **data types**. Knowing the main ones helps you understand what your code can do with each value.

## The types you will use most

**String** — text, always in quotes:

```javascript
let name = "Ada";
let greeting = 'Hello';     // single or double quotes both work
```

**Number** — any number, whole or with decimals (no quotes):

```javascript
let age = 12;
let price = 9.99;
```

**Boolean** — a yes/no value, either `true` or `false`:

```javascript
let isLoggedIn = true;
let hasPaid = false;
```

Booleans power decisions ("*if* the user is logged in…"), which you'll meet soon.

## Grouping values

**Array** — an ordered list of values in square brackets:

```javascript
let colors = ["red", "green", "blue"];
```

**Object** — a labelled collection, in curly braces:

```javascript
let person = { name: "Ada", age: 12 };
```

You will get a whole module on arrays and objects later. For now, just recognise them.

## Two "empty" types

- `undefined` — a variable that exists but has no value yet: `let x;`
- `null` — a value you deliberately set to "nothing": `let chosen = null;`

## Checking a type

Use `typeof` to ask what type a value is:

```javascript
console.log(typeof "Ada");    // "string"
console.log(typeof 12);        // "number"
console.log(typeof true);      // "boolean"
```

## Why it matters

Types change what happens. With numbers, `+` adds:

```javascript
console.log(5 + 3);        // 8
```

With strings, `+` **joins** them together (this is called *concatenation*):

```javascript
console.log("Ada" + " Lovelace");   // "Ada Lovelace"
```

Same symbol, different behaviour — because the types are different.

**Try it:** make one variable of each type (string, number, boolean) and `console.log(typeof ...)` for each.

## Where you will see this happen

Save with **Ctrl + S**, click back to the browser, press **Ctrl + R**. *(Console closed? Press **F12**, then the **Console** tab — Mac: **Command + Option + J**.)*

`typeof` prints the *kind* of value, not the value: you see `string`, `number` or `boolean` in the Console. Seeing `number` where you expected `12` means it worked.

## Recap — the short version

- `+` adds two numbers but joins two strings, so `5 + 3` gives `8` while `"5" + "3"` gives `"53"`.
- Text always sits in quotes, numbers never do. `"12"` is a string and `12` is a number, and they behave differently.
- `typeof value` tells you what kind of value you are holding — the first thing to check when something behaves oddly.
- `undefined` means a variable exists but was never given a value; `null` is a value you deliberately set to nothing.
- A boolean is only ever `true` or `false`, written without quotes.

courses.description:
> **Before this lesson,** you should be able to tell strings, numbers and booleans apart and check one with `typeof`

**Operators** are the symbols that let you *do* things with values — add them, compare them, combine them. You already used one (`=`). Here are the ones you'll use every day.

## Arithmetic (maths)

```javascript
let a = 10;
let b = 3;

console.log(a + b);   // 13  (add)
console.log(a - b);   // 7   (subtract)
console.log(a * b);   // 30  (multiply)
console.log(a / b);   // 3.33… (divide)
console.log(a % b);   // 1   (remainder — what's left over)
```

That last one, `%` (called *modulo*), gives the remainder after dividing. It's surprisingly useful — for example, `number % 2` is 0 for even numbers and 1 for odd ones.

## Assignment

`=` puts a value in a variable. There are handy shortcuts for changing a variable based on itself:

```javascript
let score = 10;
score += 5;    // same as score = score + 5   → 15
score -= 2;    // → 13
score *= 2;    // → 26
```

## Comparison — asking true/false questions

These compare two values and give back a **boolean** (`true` or `false`):

```javascript
console.log(5 > 3);     // true   (greater than)
console.log(5 < 3);     // false  (less than)
console.log(5 >= 5);    // true   (greater than or equal)
console.log(5 === 5);   // true   (exactly equal)
console.log(5 !== 3);   // true   (not equal)
```

**Important:** use `===` (three equals) to check if two things are equal, and `!==` for not-equal. (There is an older `==` with two equals — avoid it; `===` is safer because it checks the type too.)

## Logical — combining questions

- `&&` means **and** — true only if *both* sides are true.
- `||` means **or** — true if *either* side is true.
- `!` means **not** — flips true to false.

```javascript
let age = 20;
console.log(age > 12 && age < 65);   // true — it's both over 12 AND under 65
console.log(age < 10 || age > 18);   // true — the second part is true
console.log(!true);                   // false
```

These become the heart of decisions in the next module.

**Try it:** make two number variables and `console.log` their sum, their product, and whether the first is bigger than the second.

## Recap — the short version

- `===` asks *is this equal?* and `=` puts a value into a variable. Use `===` for every comparison, and `!==` for not-equal.
- `%` gives the remainder after dividing, so `number % 2` is `0` for even numbers and `1` for odd ones.
- A comparison hands back a boolean: `5 > 3` is not 5 or 3, it is `true`.
- `&&` means *and* — both sides must be true. `||` means *or* — either side will do. `!` flips true to false.
- `score += 5` is shorthand for `score = score + 5`, and `*=` and `-=` work the same way.

courses.title: Type conversion
courses.description:
> **Before this lesson,** you should be able to use arithmetic and comparison operators such as `*`, `%` and `===`

Sometimes a value is the *right* thing but the *wrong type* — a number trapped inside a string, say. **Type conversion** means turning a value from one type into another. It's a small topic that fixes a lot of real bugs.

## The classic bug: numbers as text

Values typed by a user, or read from a web page, almost always arrive as **strings** — even if they look like numbers. Watch what goes wrong:

```javascript
let a = "5";
let b = "3";
console.log(a + b);    // "53"  — NOT 8!
```

Because `a` and `b` are strings, `+` **joins** them instead of adding. This trips up every beginner. The fix is to convert them to numbers first.

## Turn a string into a number

Use `Number(...)`:

```javascript
let a = "5";
let b = "3";
console.log(Number(a) + Number(b));   // 8  ✓
```

Two shortcuts you'll also see:
- `parseInt("5")` → `5` (whole numbers)
- `parseFloat("9.99")` → `9.99` (decimals)

## Turn a number into a string

Use `String(...)`:

```javascript
let age = 12;
let message = "You are " + String(age) + " years old";
console.log(message);   // "You are 12 years old"
```

(In practice, joining a number to a string with `+` converts it automatically, but `String(...)` makes your intent clear.)

## Truthy and falsy

JavaScript can treat non-boolean values as true/false in a yes/no context. These count as **false**: `false`, `0`, `""` (empty string), `null`, `undefined`. Almost everything else counts as **true**. You'll use this in conditions:

```javascript
let name = "";
if (name) {
  console.log("Has a name");
} else {
  console.log("Name is empty");   // this runs — "" is falsy
}
```

## The lesson to remember

When maths gives you a weird joined-up result like `"53"`, you have a string where you wanted a number. Wrap it in `Number(...)`.

**Try it:** make two string variables `"7"` and `"8"`, and `console.log` their sum as a real number (15), using `Number(...)`.

## Recap — the short version

- When a sum prints a joined-up answer like `"53"` instead of `8`, you have strings where you wanted numbers. Wrap each one in `Number(...)`.
- Anything a person types into a page arrives as a string, even when it looks like a number.
- `Number("5")` gives the number `5`; `String(12)` gives the text `"12"`.
- `parseInt("5")` reads a whole number out of a string and `parseFloat("9.99")` reads a decimal.
- These count as false in a yes/no test: `false`, `0`, `""`, `null` and `undefined`. Almost everything else counts as true.

courses.title: Looping over items
courses.description:
> **Before this lesson,** you should be able to repeat a block of code with a `for` or a `while` loop

A plain `for` loop counts with a number. But very often you just want to go through **every item in a list** — every name, every price, every to-do. JavaScript has friendlier loops for exactly that. (You'll meet lists — *arrays* — properly in the next module; here we just loop over one.)

## `for...of` — go through each item

The cleanest way to visit every item in a list:

```javascript
const colors = ["red", "green", "blue"];

for (const color of colors) {
  console.log(color);
}
```

Read it as: *"for each color of colors, do this."* Each time round, `color` holds the next item. It prints red, then green, then blue — no counting, no `i`, no index to get wrong.

It works on text too, letter by letter:

```javascript
for (const letter of "cat") {
  console.log(letter);   // c, a, t
}
```

## `forEach` — the list does the looping

Lists also have a built-in `forEach` that runs a piece of code for every item:

```javascript
const scores = [10, 20, 30];

scores.forEach(function (score) {
  console.log(score);
});
```

For each item, the function runs with that item as `score`. This style becomes very natural once you've seen it a few times.

## Which should I use?

- **`for...of`** — simplest to read; great default for "do something with each item."
- **`forEach`** — common in real code, especially alongside the array tools you'll learn next.
- **plain `for`** — when you truly need the counting number (position) itself.

They all achieve the same goal: touch every item once.

**Try it:** make a list of three of your favourite foods and use `for...of` to `console.log` each one.

## Recap — the short version

- `for (const color of colors)` visits every item in turn and hands it to you as `color` — no counter and no index to get wrong.
- `for...of` works on text too, giving you one letter at a time.
- `forEach` runs a function once per item and the whole thing is one statement: `list.forEach(function (item) { ... });` — watch the closing `});`.
- Reach for a plain `for` loop only when you need the position number itself.

A script that counts from 1 to 10 and, for each number, says whether it is **even** or **odd**. It uses a loop (to repeat) and an `if / else` (to decide) — the two ideas from this module working together.

Remember the remainder operator `%` from the operators lesson? A number is **even** when dividing it by 2 leaves no remainder:

courses.description:

A **string** is text — a name, a message, a whole paragraph. You've used them since lesson one. Now let's see what you can *do* with them, because strings come with a toolbox of built-in helpers.

## Making strings

Single or double quotes both work:

```javascript
let a = "Hello";
let b = 'World';
```

## Joining strings

Two ways. The old way, with `+`:

```javascript
let name = "Ada";
console.log("Hello, " + name + "!");   // Hello, Ada!
```

The modern, cleaner way — **template literals**, using back-ticks `` ` `` and `${...}`:

```javascript
let name = "Ada";
console.log(`Hello, ${name}!`);        // Hello, Ada!
```

Inside back-ticks, anything in `${...}` is worked out and dropped into the text. Much easier to read than lots of `+`. Use this from now on.

## String length

Every string knows how long it is, via `.length`:

```javascript
let word = "banana";
console.log(word.length);   // 6
```

## Useful string methods

A **method** is an action you call with a dot and brackets. Strings have lots:

```javascript
let s = "Hello World";

console.log(s.toUpperCase());     // "HELLO WORLD"
console.log(s.toLowerCase());     // "hello world"
console.log(s.includes("World")); // true  — does it contain this?
console.log(s.indexOf("W"));      // 6     — position of "W"
console.log(s.replace("World", "there")); // "Hello there"
console.log(s.slice(0, 5));       // "Hello" — characters 0 up to 5
console.log(s.trim());            // removes spaces at the ends
```

You don't need to memorise these — just know the *shape*: `theString.method(...)`. You'll look up the exact name when you need it.

## Strings are counted from 0

Positions ("indexes") start at **0**, not 1. In "Hello", `H` is at 0, `e` at 1, and so on. This 0-based counting appears everywhere in programming.

**Try it:** make a string with your full name, then `console.log` its `.length` and its `.toUpperCase()`.

## Recap — the short version

- Positions in a string are counted from **0**, so in `"Hello"` the `H` is at 0 and the `o` is at 4.
- Template literals use back-ticks and `${...}`: `` `Hello, ${name}!` ``. A back-tick, not an apostrophe — it usually shares a key with `~`.
- `.length` is a property and takes no brackets; `.toUpperCase()` is a method and needs its brackets.
- String methods hand back a *new* string and leave the original alone, so `s.toUpperCase()` does not change `s`.
- You are not meant to memorise the method names. Learn the shape, `theString.method(...)`, and look the rest up.

JavaScript has one type for all numbers — whole ones like `12` and decimals like `9.99` are both just **numbers**. This lesson covers the handy things you can do with them.

## Whole numbers and decimals

```javascript
let whole = 42;
let decimal = 3.14;
```

No commas in big numbers — write `1000000`, not `1,000,000`.

## Rounding to a fixed number of decimals

Money usually needs exactly two decimal places. `toFixed` does that:

```javascript
let price = 9.5;
console.log(price.toFixed(2));   // "9.50"
```

Note: `toFixed` gives back a **string** (nicely formatted), which is perfect for showing to people.

## Turning text into numbers (recap)

Values from forms arrive as strings. Convert them before doing maths:

```javascript
let typed = "25";
console.log(Number(typed) + 5);   // 30
```

`parseInt("25")` (whole) and `parseFloat("9.99")` (decimal) do similar jobs.

## NaN — "Not a Number"

If you try to turn nonsense into a number, you get `NaN`:

```javascript
console.log(Number("hello"));    // NaN
```

`NaN` means *"that wasn't a valid number."* If your calculations show `NaN`, you probably have text where you expected a number — check your conversions.

## Infinity

Divide by zero and JavaScript doesn't crash — it gives `Infinity`:

```javascript
console.log(5 / 0);    // Infinity
```

## Quick checks

```javascript
console.log(Number.isInteger(10));    // true  — is it a whole number?
console.log(Number.isInteger(10.5));  // false
```

**Try it:** make a price like `12.3456`, and `console.log` it rounded to 2 decimals with `.toFixed(2)`.

## Recap — the short version

- `.toFixed(2)` hands back a **string**, not a number. It is made for showing a price, not for doing more maths with it.
- `NaN` means *not a number*: you did maths on something that was not a number. Check your conversions.
- Write big numbers with no commas — `1000000`, not `1,000,000`.
- Dividing by zero gives `Infinity` rather than an error, so a result of `Infinity` points at a zero you did not expect.
- `Number.isInteger(10.5)` is `false` — a quick way to ask whether a number is whole.

courses.description:
> **Before this lesson,** you should be able to round a number to two decimal places with `.toFixed(2)`

`Math` is a built-in toolbox for number work — rounding, random numbers, powers, and more. You don't create it or import it; it's just always there. You call its tools with `Math.` in front.

## Rounding

```javascript
console.log(Math.round(4.6));   // 5   — to the nearest whole
console.log(Math.floor(4.9));   // 4   — always DOWN
console.log(Math.ceil(4.1));    // 5   — always UP
console.log(Math.trunc(4.9));   // 4   — just chop off the decimal
```

`floor` and `ceil` are easy to remember: the *floor* is below you, the *ceiling* is above you.

## Biggest and smallest

```javascript
console.log(Math.max(3, 8, 2));   // 8
console.log(Math.min(3, 8, 2));   // 2
```

## Powers and roots

```javascript
console.log(Math.pow(2, 3));   // 8   — 2 to the power of 3
console.log(2 ** 3);            // 8   — shorter way to write the same
console.log(Math.sqrt(16));    // 4   — square root
console.log(Math.abs(-7));     // 7   — distance from zero (always positive)
```

## Random numbers

`Math.random()` gives a random decimal between 0 and 1 (never quite 1):

```javascript
console.log(Math.random());    // e.g. 0.4172…
```

On its own that's rarely what you want. The usual recipe for a random **whole number** from 1 to a maximum:

```javascript
let max = 6;
let roll = Math.floor(Math.random() * max) + 1;
console.log(roll);   // a dice roll: 1 to 6
```

Read it inside-out: random decimal → times 6 → floor to a whole 0–5 → add 1 to get 1–6. This exact pattern powers dice, card shuffles, and "pick a random item."

**Try it:** print a random dice roll (1 to 6), and print the largest of three numbers using `Math.max`.

## Where you will see this happen

A random number only proves itself when you watch it change.

1. Save with **Ctrl + S**, click back to the browser and press **Ctrl + R**.
2. Read the dice roll in the Console. It is a whole number from 1 to 6.
3. Press **Ctrl + R** again. And again, four or five times.

The number changes on most reloads and sometimes repeats, exactly as a real die does. If it never changes at all, check you have written `Math.random()` with its brackets.

*(Console closed? Press **F12**, then click the **Console** tab — Mac: **Command + Option + J**.)*

## Recap — the short version

- `Math.floor(Math.random() * max) + 1` is the recipe for a whole number from 1 to `max`. Learn the shape; the reasoning follows later.
- `Math.random()` gives a decimal between 0 and 1 and never quite reaches 1.
- `Math.floor` always rounds down, `Math.ceil` always rounds up, and `Math.round` goes to the nearest.
- `Math` is always there. You never create it or import it — write `Math.` in front of the tool you want.
- `Math.max(3, 8, 2)` takes values separated by commas, not a list.

courses.description:

Websites constantly work with **dates and times** — "posted 2 hours ago," a countdown, today's date on a dashboard. JavaScript handles all of this with the built-in `Date`.

## Getting the current date and time

You make a date with `new Date()`. With nothing in the brackets, you get **right now**:

```javascript
let now = new Date();
console.log(now);   // e.g. Wed Sep 17 2026 09:23:00 ...
```

## Reading pieces out of a date

A date knows its year, month, day, hour, and so on. You read each with a `get` method:

```javascript
let now = new Date();

console.log(now.getFullYear());   // 2026
console.log(now.getMonth());      // 0–11  (careful: January is 0!)
console.log(now.getDate());       // day of the month, 1–31
console.log(now.getHours());      // 0–23
console.log(now.getMinutes());    // 0–59
console.log(now.getDay());        // day of the week, 0 (Sun) – 6 (Sat)
```

Two things surprise everyone at first:
- **Months start at 0**, so `getMonth()` returns 8 for September.
- `getDate()` is the day *number* (like 17); `getDay()` is the *weekday* (0–6).

## Making a specific date

Put the parts in the brackets (remember month is 0-based):

```javascript
let birthday = new Date(2010, 5, 21);   // 21 June 2010  (5 = June)
console.log(birthday.getFullYear());     // 2010
```

## A friendly string

```javascript
let now = new Date();
console.log(now.toDateString());     // "Wed Sep 17 2026"
console.log(now.toLocaleDateString()); // "17/09/2026" — in your local format
```

**Try it:** make `let now = new Date()` and `console.log` the current year and the current hour.

## Recap — the short version

- Months are counted from 0, so `getMonth()` gives `8` for September and `11` for December.
- `getDate()` is the day of the month (1–31); `getDay()` is the day of the week (0 for Sunday to 6 for Saturday).
- `new Date()` with empty brackets means *right now*, so what prints depends on the moment it runs and on the computer it runs on. Yours will not match the example.
- Building a specific date takes the month from 0 as well: `new Date(2010, 5, 21)` is 21 June 2010.
- `toDateString()` gives a readable version, and `toLocaleDateString()` follows the date format the computer is set to.

courses.description:
> **Before this lesson,** you should be able to store single values in variables and loop over items with `for...of`

An **array** is an ordered list of values, all held in one variable. Instead of `color1`, `color2`, `color3`, you keep them together in a single list. Arrays are one of the most useful tools in all of programming.

## Making an array

Square brackets, values separated by commas:

```javascript
let colors = ["red", "green", "blue"];
let scores = [10, 20, 30];
let mixed  = ["Ada", 12, true];   // types can mix, though usually they don't
```

## Getting items out — by position

Each item has an **index** (a position number), starting at **0**:

```javascript
let colors = ["red", "green", "blue"];

console.log(colors[0]);   // "red"   — the first
console.log(colors[1]);   // "green" — the second
console.log(colors[2]);   // "blue"  — the third
```

`colors[0]` is the first item — 0, not 1. This catches everyone out at first, so say it to yourself: *the first item is at index zero.*

## How many items?

```javascript
console.log(colors.length);   // 3
```

A handy trick: the last item is always at `length - 1`:

```javascript
console.log(colors[colors.length - 1]);   // "blue"
```

## Changing items

Arrays made with `let` (or even `const`) can have their contents changed:

```javascript
let colors = ["red", "green", "blue"];
colors[1] = "yellow";
console.log(colors);   // ["red", "yellow", "blue"]
```

## Adding and removing at the end

```javascript
let colors = ["red", "green"];
colors.push("blue");    // add to the end     → ["red","green","blue"]
colors.pop();           // remove from the end → ["red","green"]
```

`push` and `pop` are the two you'll use most.

## Looping over an array

Combine arrays with the loops you already know:

```javascript
let colors = ["red", "green", "blue"];
for (const color of colors) {
  console.log(color);
}
```

**Try it:** make an array of your three favourite foods, `console.log` the first one and the `.length`, then `push` a fourth food.

## Recap — the short version

- Counting starts at zero. In `["red", "green", "blue"]`, `colors[0]` is `"red"`, `colors[1]` is `"green"` and `colors[2]` is `"blue"`. There is no `colors[3]` — asking for it gives `undefined`.
- `.length` counts from 1, which is why the last item is always at `length - 1`: `colors[colors.length - 1]`.
- `push` adds an item to the end and `pop` removes the last one.
- An array made with `const` can still have its contents changed. `const` protects the box, not what is inside it.
- Change an item by its position: `colors[1] = "yellow"` replaces the second item.

> **Before this lesson,** you should be able to transform or select items from an array with `map` and `filter`

Arrays are the list you'll reach for 90% of the time. But JavaScript has two more collection types worth meeting: **Set** (a list with no duplicates) and **Map** (a set of labelled pairs). You won't use them daily, but knowing they exist saves you reinventing them.

## Set — a list of unique values

A **Set** automatically ignores duplicates. Add the same thing twice and it only keeps one:

```javascript
const tags = new Set();
tags.add("news");
tags.add("sport");
tags.add("news");     // ignored — already there

console.log(tags.size);          // 2
console.log(tags.has("sport"));  // true
```

A neat trick: turn an array into a Set to **remove duplicates**, then back into an array:

```javascript
const withDupes = [1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3];
const unique = [...new Set(withDupes)];
console.log(unique);   // [1, 2, 3]
```

(The `...` "spreads" the Set's items back into a new array — a handy piece of syntax.)

## Map — labelled pairs

A **Map** stores values under keys (labels), a bit like a dictionary: look up a word, get its meaning.

```javascript
const ages = new Map();
ages.set("Ada", 12);
ages.set("Grace", 15);

console.log(ages.get("Ada"));    // 12
console.log(ages.has("Grace"));  // true
console.log(ages.size);          // 2
```

## Set or Map or... just an array/object?

- Need a simple list, order matters, duplicates OK → **array**.
- Need a list where every value must be unique → **Set**.
- Need to look things up by a label → **Map** (or an **object**, which you'll meet next module and use more often).

Don't overthink it. For now, just recognise `new Set()` and `new Map()` when you see them, and remember the one everyday use: a Set removes duplicates.

**Try it:** make a `Set` from the array `[1, 1, 2, 3, 3]` and `console.log` its `.size` (it should be 3).

## Recap — the short version

- A `Set` quietly ignores a value it already holds, which is why it is the everyday way to remove duplicates.
- Sets and Maps use `.size`, not `.length`. Asking a Set for `.length` gives `undefined`.
- `[...new Set(list)]` turns a list into a Set and back into an array, with the duplicates gone.
- A Map stores values under labels: `.set(key, value)` puts one in and `.get(key)` takes it out.
- Both are created with `new` — `new Set()` and `new Map()`.

courses.description:

**Scope** is a simple but important idea: it's the answer to the question *"where can this variable be seen?"* Getting it means fewer confusing bugs where a variable "doesn't exist" or "has the wrong value."

## Variables live where you make them

A variable made **inside** a function only exists inside that function. The outside world can't see it:

```javascript
function greet() {
  let message = "Hello";
  console.log(message);   // works — we're inside
}

greet();
console.log(message);     // Error! "message" doesn't exist out here
```

`message` is **local** to `greet`. When the function finishes, it's gone. This is a good thing — each function keeps its own little workspace and can't accidentally trip over another's variables.

## Global variables

A variable made **outside** all functions is **global** — everything can see it:

```javascript
let siteName = "LaceFi Academy";

function showName() {
  console.log(siteName);   // works — globals are visible inside too
}
showName();
```

Use globals sparingly. Too many, and any part of your code could change them, which gets messy.

## Block scope

`let` and `const` are also limited to the `{ }` block they're in — including an `if` or a loop:

```javascript
if (true) {
  let secret = 42;
}
console.log(secret);   // Error! "secret" only existed inside the if-block
```

This is another reason to prefer `let`/`const` over the old `var` (which ignored block scope and caused surprises).

## The rule of thumb

*Make a variable in the smallest place that needs it.* Need it only inside a function? Declare it there. Need it inside a loop only? Declare it in the loop. Keep things local, and reach for a global only when something truly must be shared everywhere.

**Try it:** make a function with a local variable, `console.log` it inside the function (works), then try to log it outside (see the error).

## Recap — the short version

- A variable made inside a function exists only inside it. Logging it outside gives an error — that error is the rule working, not a typing fault.
- `let` and `const` are also trapped inside whatever `{ }` block they are in, including an `if` block or a loop body.
- A variable made outside every function is global and can be seen everywhere, including inside functions. Keep the number of globals small.
- Make each variable in the smallest place that needs it: inside the loop if only the loop uses it, inside the function if only the function does.
- This block behaviour is one reason to use `let` and `const` rather than the older `var`, which ignored it.

courses.title: Arrow functions
courses.description:
> **Before this lesson,** you should be able to write a function with the `function` keyword and call it by name

**Arrow functions** are a shorter way to write functions. They do the same job as the `function` you already learned — just with less typing. You'll see them constantly in real code, so it's worth getting comfortable with the shape.

## From `function` to arrow

Here's a normal function:

```javascript
function double(n) {
  return n * 2;
}
```

Here's the exact same thing as an arrow function:

```javascript
const double = (n) => {
  return n * 2;
};
```

What changed:
- The word `function` is gone.
- The function is stored in a variable (`const double = ...`).
- An **arrow** `=>` sits between the inputs and the body.

You call it the same way: `double(8)` → `16`.

## The short form

When a function just returns one thing, you can drop the `{ }` and the `return`:

```javascript
const double = (n) => n * 2;
const add = (a, b) => a + b;

console.log(double(5));   // 10
console.log(add(2, 3));   // 5
```

Short and clean. With one parameter you can even drop its brackets: `n => n * 2`.

## Where you'll see them most

Arrow functions shine inside array methods like `map` and `filter`:

```javascript
const nums = [1, 2, 3, 4];

const doubled = nums.map(n => n * 2);      // [2, 4, 6, 8]
const evens   = nums.filter(n => n % 2 === 0);  // [2, 4]

console.log(doubled, evens);
```

Compare that to writing `function (n) { return ... }` each time — the arrow version is much easier to read.

## Which should I use?

Both are fine. Many developers use arrows for short one-liners (especially inside `map`/`filter`) and the `function` keyword for bigger, named functions. Learn to recognise both; you'll drift to your own style with practice.

**Try it:** rewrite `function triple(n) { return n * 3; }` as a short arrow function, then `console.log(triple(4))`.

## Recap — the short version

- An arrow function is stored in a variable, so its name comes before the `=`: `const double = (n) => n * 2;`
- The arrow is `=>` — an equals sign then a greater-than sign, with nothing between them.
- With no `{ }`, the one expression is returned for you. Put the braces back and you must write `return` yourself again.
- An arrow function does the same job as one written with `function`; both are correct and you will meet both.
- You will see arrows most often inside `map` and `filter`, where the short form keeps the line readable.
